```{r}
# Create a sample data frame of payment amounts
# These values are designed to roughly follow Benford's Law.
set.seed(123)
payments <- data.frame(
  amount = rlnorm(500, meanlog = 5, sdlog = 2)
)

# View the first few rows
head(payments)
```


The module's own analysis takes exactly two options: `var` (the numeric variable) and
`digits` (how many leading digits to analyse; default `2`).

```{r}
library(ClinicoPathDescriptives)

results <- benford(
    data   = payments,
    var    = "amount",
    digits = 2      # default is 2
)

# Result items available on the returned object:
results$text   # Preformatted: benford.analysis print output
results$text2  # Preformatted: suspect records
results$plot   # Image: digit-distribution plot
```

For full control over the underlying computation you can also call the
`benford.analysis` package directly:

```{r}
# NOTE: `benford()` below is benford.analysis::benford(), which has a different
# signature to ClinicoPathDescriptives::benford(). Attach the packages in this order,
# or qualify the call, to avoid masking.

# Load required library
library(benford.analysis)

# Check the data structure
str(payments)
print(head(payments))

# Run the Benford analysis using the benford.analysis package directly
bfd.cp <- benford(data = payments$amount)

# View the results
print(bfd.cp)

# Create plot
plot(bfd.cp)

# Get suspects
suspects <- getSuspects(bfd.cp, payments)
if(length(suspects) > 0) {
  print("Suspicious values:")
  print(suspects)
} else {
  print("No suspicious values detected")
}
```
